plain: Should gun laws be stricter than they are now? Colorado added a permit-and-training rule for many semiautomatic guns on August 1, 2026.

short_version.text: Colorado already has a three-day wait, a minimum buying age of 21, red-flag orders and, since August 2026, a permit and training rule for many semiautomatic guns. Most gun deaths in Colorado are suicides. Research supports some laws, such as background checks and waiting periods, more than others, and the new permit rule faces a court challenge.

agree_means: Supports more gun restrictions, such as Colorado's SB25-003 permit rule, wider background checks or bans on certain guns.
disagree_means: Opposes new restrictions or wants to loosen current ones, saying existing laws are enough or that new limits burden lawful owners.

example.text: Someone buying a covered semiautomatic rifle in Colorado now needs a sheriff-issued eligibility card, a background check and a 4- or 12-hour safety course, plus a $52 state fee.

now.text: Colorado law already has a three-day wait to take delivery of a gun. The minimum age to buy a gun is 21 (since August 2023). Red flag orders, in place since 2020, let a court temporarily remove guns from someone judged a serious risk.

sources.title: HB19-1177 Extreme risk protection order, bill summary (Colorado General Assembly)
sources.quote: The act creates the ability for a family or household member or a law enforcement officer to petition the court for a temporary extreme risk protection order (ERPO) beginning on January 1, 2020.

now.text: SB25-003 took effect August 1, 2026. Buying certain semiautomatic rifles, shotguns and pistols with detachable magazines now requires a sheriff-issued eligibility card, a background check and a 4- or 12-hour safety course. The state fee is $52.

now.text: Johns Hopkins researchers counted 961 gun deaths in Colorado in 2024. In 2023, about 71% of the state's 1,012 gun deaths were suicides. The gun homicide rate rose 40% from 2015 to 2024.

stakes.text: RAND, a nonprofit research group, reviewed the studies in January 2026. It found moderate evidence that background checks decrease homicides and limited evidence that permit rules do. Evidence on training requirements is inconclusive. Bans on high-capacity magazines show limited evidence of fewer mass-shooting deaths.

stakes.text: Suicide drives Colorado's gun death numbers. RAND finds moderate evidence that waiting periods decrease gun suicides and supportive evidence that a purchase age of 21 lowers youth gun suicides. Evidence on red flag orders and suicide is limited.

stakes.text: Buyers of covered guns pay more. The state fee is $52, sheriffs may add local fees, and one buyer reported a 12-hour course costs $500. Johns Hopkins researchers estimate gun violence cost Coloradans $10.2 billion in 2024.

research_notes: Claude in Chrome was not connected, so the Johns Hopkins Center for Gun Violence Solutions state page (Cloudflare-blocked) was read in the built-in Browser pane; its source carries via: browser. Other pages were fetched directly. Double-check: (1) The Johns Hopkins page also lists 712 gun suicides and 209 gun homicides for 2024 in separate page elements, so those numbers are not quoted; the 71% suicide share is for 2023 (Colorado Sun, using state health data). (2) RAND evidence ratings are from its Jan 29, 2026 update; the RAND gun-policy project has since wound down. The ratings describe studies of laws elsewhere; none test Colorado's SB25-003 yet. (3) The Gazette lawsuit story is a Center Square wire piece; the Aug 10, 2026 court filing (Del Toro v. Polis) shows the case is ongoing and that plaintiffs planned to seek a preliminary injunction; whether a ruling has issued was not checked. (4) Colorado's 2013 background-check and magazine laws, safe-storage and other laws were not sourced and are not described. (5) The $500 course price is one buyer's statement in the Gazette, not an official fee. The state fee ($52) is stated by the Gazette. (6) The SCOTUSblog piece is commentary on Wolford and Hemani; its note that Wolford casts doubt on lower-court rulings is the author's view. (7) The web-search allowance ran out mid-run; some leads (Montezuma County sheriff refusing to issue cards, the Colorado Newsline Aug 4 article) were not fetched and are not used.
